forward.prompt:
These are every image in one clothing SKU. Each VIEW contains an original photograph and a sheet of its SAM3 mask regions. Every mask has a UNIQUE ID beginning with R; IDs never repeat in another view.
Find every visually distinct garment that has visible pixels in an available mask in EVERY VIEW. The same garment may be shown alone, worn, from behind, as a fabric detail, or partly hidden under another layer. Use ALL views to establish identity. Do not require a small visible collar or undershirt strip to have the full garment silhouette. Match by fabric, construction, color and the context. A jacket and its undershirt remain separate garments even if the layers are sewn together. Similar colors alone are insufficient. A mask mixing different garments is not usable. Do not invent unseen pixels or new mask boundaries.
First describe which garments are present and which disappear, using the region IDs printed on the crops. Then output JSON: {"tracks":[{"garment":"description","regions":["R001", "R004", ...]}]}. This is only an output schema, not an answer. List only supplied region IDs and assign each ID to at most one track. A track must cover EVERY VIEW with at least one visible region. Extra fragments of the SAME garment in a view may share a track. Unlisted regions are removed. Keep repeated styling too, if present in every view. Do not select by the item for sale. If nothing is visibly supported everywhere, return an empty tracks list.
forward.raw:
In each of the three views (v0, v1, v2), we are given an original photograph showing three garments arranged side-by-side, and a corresponding set of mask regions (R001–R003 for v0, R004–R006 for v1, R007–R009 for v2). Each mask region corresponds to one of the garments in the photograph.

We are to identify garments that appear in **every view**, using the mask regions as evidence. The mask regions are labeled and correspond to specific garments in each view. Since each view has three garments, and each mask region is unique to that view (no ID repeats across views), we can map the garments across views by their visual characteristics.

---

### Step 1: Identify garments in each view

**VIEW v0:**
- R001: Brown, long-sleeved, cut-out top (left)
- R002: Black, halter-style top with keyhole cutout (middle)
- R003: Black, zip-up leather jacket (right)

**VIEW v1:**
- R004: Brown, long-sleeved, cut-out top (left) — visually identical to R001
- R005: Black, halter-style top with keyhole cutout (middle) — visually identical to R002
- R006: Black, zip-up leather jacket (right) — visually identical to R003

**VIEW v2:**
- R007: Brown, long-sleeved, cut-out top (left) — visually identical to R001 and R004
- R008: Black, halter-style top with keyhole cutout (middle) — visually identical to R002 and R005
- R009: Black, zip-up leather jacket (right) — visually identical to R003 and R006

---

### Step 2: Track garments across all views

We must assign each region to a garment track, ensuring that the garment is visually consistent across all views.

- **Brown cut-out top**: Appears in R001 (v0), R004 (v1), R007 (v2) — same fabric, cut, color, style → **one track**
- **Black halter top**: Appears in R002 (v0), R005 (v1), R008 (v2) — same fabric, cut, color, style → **one track**
- **Black leather jacket**: Appears in R003 (v0), R006 (v1), R009 (v2) — same fabric, cut, color, style → **one track**

All three garments are present in every view, and each is uniquely identifiable by its visual characteristics and mask region.

---

### Step 3: Output JSON

```json
{
  "tracks": [
    {
      "garment": "Brown long-sleeved cut-out top",
      "regions": ["R001", "R004", "R007"]
    },
    {
      "garment": "Black halter-style top with keyhole cutout",
      "regions": ["R002", "R005", "R008"]
    },
    {
      "garment": "Black zip-up leather jacket",
      "regions": ["R003", "R006", "R009"]
    }
  ]
}
```
